title: First Aid & Safety · Episode 5
chapters: Electricity: the danger you can't see

units.t: First Aid & Safety. Episode five.
In this episode: Carbon monoxide: the invisible killer, Electricity: the danger you can't see and Staying alive on long drives.
Part one. Carbon monoxide: the invisible killer.
It has no colour, no smell and no taste, and its symptoms feel like the flu.
Here is how an ordinary heater can quietly poison a home, and how to stop it.
Two brothers.
In May 2010, two brothers, Chase and Tyler Robinson, died in their sleep at their rented home in Mooroopna, near Shepparton in Victoria.
The cause was carbon monoxide from a faulty gas heater.
Nothing had seemed wrong: no smoke, no strange smell, and no alarm, because the home had no carbon monoxide detector.
A coronial inquest examined who was responsible for maintaining the heater.
Their mother, Vanessa Robinson, became a prominent campaigner for gas heater safety, and Victoria has since introduced regular gas safety checks in rental homes.
It is a painful reminder that the most dangerous hazards may be ones we cannot sense.
How it harms.
Carbon monoxide is made when fuels such as gas, wood, charcoal, petrol or diesel burn without enough oxygen.
Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin.
Carbon monoxide binds to it roughly two hundred times more strongly than oxygen does, so even small amounts steadily push oxygen out of the blood.
The brain and heart suffer first.
The gas is colourless, odourless and tasteless, so people breathe it unaware.
High levels can cause unconsciousness and death within minutes.
Lower levels over hours or days can cause lasting brain and heart damage.
Symptoms that fool.
Early symptoms are ordinary: headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, tiredness, weakness, breathlessness and confusion.
People assume flu, migraine or a stomach bug.
Clues point to carbon monoxide instead.
Several people, or pets, feel sick at once.
Symptoms are worse at home or with a heater running, and improve outside.
People who are asleep or have been drinking may lose consciousness before noticing, so night-time poisoning is especially dangerous.
Babies, older people, pregnant women and people with heart or lung disease are more vulnerable.
Sources and servicing.
A major source in Australian homes is gas space heaters, especially older or poorly maintained ones.
An open-flued heater should send fumes out through a flue, but a blocked or faulty flue, or exhaust fans pulling air the wrong way, can spill carbon monoxide inside.
Unflued heaters release fumes into the room and need good ventilation.
Other causes are barbecues, camping stoves, patio heaters or charcoal used indoors, in tents, caravans or garages, generators near open windows, and engines running in closed garages.
Have gas heaters serviced by a licensed gasfitter, generally at least every two years or as the manufacturer recommends.
Warning signs include a yellow or orange flame, soot or stains, and a stuffy room.
If you rent, ask when the heater was last checked.
Alarms and action.
Smoke alarms don't detect carbon monoxide.
A separate alarm from a hardware store warns you when levels rise.
Place it per the instructions, typically near fuel-burning appliances and sleeping areas, and test it regularly.
Requirements for them vary by state and territory, but regulators encourage them, especially with gas heating.
An alarm is a backstop, not a substitute for servicing.
If you suspect poisoning, get everyone, including pets, into fresh air.
If quick and safe, switch off the appliance and open doors on your way out.
Call 000.
Start CPR if someone isn't breathing normally.
Don't return until a licensed gasfitter has checked the source.
Treatment is high-concentration oxygen, and everyone should be assessed.
The key idea: Two young brothers died in 2010 from a faulty gas heater, with no smoke, smell or alarm to warn them.
Part two. Electricity: the danger you can't see.
Electricity gives no warning: no smell, no sound, nothing to see.
A few simple rules, and one small switch in your meter box, stand between ordinary life and a fatal shock.
Why current kills.
Current crossing the chest can throw the heart into a chaotic rhythm called ventricular fibrillation, where it quivers instead of pumping.
That is cardiac arrest.
Current can also make muscles contract so strongly a person can't let go of what they're holding.
And as it passes through tissue, it generates heat and burns along its path.
Entry and exit wounds can look small while muscles, nerves and blood vessels inside are badly damaged.
Anyone who has had a significant shock or electrical burn should be checked by a doctor, even if they feel fine.
Safety switches.
A residual current device, called a safety switch in Australia, constantly compares the current going out along the active wire with the current returning along the neutral.
If they don't match, current is leaking somewhere, possibly through a person.
The switch cuts the power within a fraction of a second, fast enough to greatly reduce the risk of death.
Safety switches differ from circuit breakers and fuses, which mainly protect wiring from overload.
Newer homes must have them, but many older homes have them on only some circuits, or none.
Most have a test button worth pressing regularly.
Leave it to licensed.
Across Australia, it's illegal for an unlicensed person to do electrical wiring work, such as installing power points, replacing light switches or running cables.
Faulty wiring can kill, sometimes years later and for someone else entirely, and a loose connection can start a fire inside a wall.
At home, the habits are simple.
Don't use appliances with frayed or damaged cords.
Don't overload power boards or daisy-chain them.
Keep appliances away from water and never touch switches with wet hands.
Never fish toast from a plugged-in toaster with a knife.
If a switch or power point feels warm or smells of burning, get it checked.
Powerlines down.
After storms, crashes and bushfires, powerlines can lie on the ground, fences, cars or trees.
Treat every fallen line as live, even if it isn't sparking, because it may be re-energised automatically.
Distributors advise staying at least eight metres away, about two car lengths.
Electricity can travel through wet ground, puddles, fences and metal, so you needn't touch the line to be hurt.
Call 000 if someone is injured or there's a fire.
If a line falls on your car, stay inside unless it's on fire.
If you must leave, jump clear with your feet together, never touching the car and ground at the same time, then shuffle away with small steps.
Helping, and looking up.
If someone is being electrocuted, don't grab them.
The current can flow into you too.
Switch off the power at the switchboard or wall, or unplug the appliance if safe.
For powerlines and high voltage, don't approach: call 000 and wait for the electricity company.
Once power is off, check them using DRSABCD, start CPR if needed, send for a defibrillator and cool burns under cool running water for twenty minutes.
Many serious accidents happen outdoors when tall objects meet overhead lines: ladders, tipper trays, boat masts.
Electricity can also arc across a gap.
Look up before raising anything tall, carry long objects horizontally, and never climb poles, towers or train roofs.
The key idea: Electric current can stop the heart and cause deep burns that look small from outside.
Part three. Staying alive on long drives.
Australia's long, empty roads are beautiful, but fatigue, wildlife and remote breakdowns catch out even experienced drivers.
Here is how to make every road trip end safely.
The hypnotic road.
There is something hypnotic about a long Australian highway: straight bitumen, red dirt, a horizon that never gets closer.
That is part of the danger.
Most Australians live in cities, yet a large share of road deaths happen on rural and regional roads, often in single-vehicle crashes where a car leaves the road or hits a tree.
Speeds are higher, roads may be narrow or unsealed, and help can be hours away.
Road safety campaigns talk about the 'fatal five': speeding, drink and drug driving, not wearing a seatbelt, fatigue and distraction.
On long drives the last two matter most, because they creep up on people who felt fine when they set out.
Fatigue and microsleeps.
Being awake for a long time impairs reactions and judgement in a way research has compared to having alcohol in your blood.
The scariest part is the microsleep: a few seconds when your brain switches off, often without you realising.
At 100 kilometres per hour a car covers nearly 28 metres every second, so a four-second microsleep carries you well over 100 metres with nobody in control.
Warning signs include yawning, heavy eyes, drifting in your lane, missing signs and not remembering the last few kilometres.
Opening the window or turning up the music does not fix tiredness.
The only real cure is sleep, so pull over somewhere safe for a rest or a power nap.
Planning to beat fatigue.
Fatigue is far easier to prevent than to fight.
Start a long drive well rested, and avoid setting out after a full day of work or when your body normally sleeps, such as late at night and in the mid-afternoon slump.
Road safety agencies commonly recommend a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours.
Get out, walk around, and have a drink and a snack.
Look for Driver Reviver sites, which often operate on major highways in holiday periods and offer free tea, coffee and a chat.
If you can, share the driving with another licensed driver.
Be honest about how far you can go.
An extra night in a motel is a small price compared with the cost of a crash.
Animals, trains and gravel.
Kangaroos, wallabies, wombats, emus and livestock are a real hazard, especially at dawn, dusk and night.
Slow down where wildlife signs appear and scan the verges for eyes reflecting your headlights.
If an animal jumps out, brake firmly in a straight line.
Many serious crashes happen when drivers swerve, lose control and hit a tree or oncoming vehicle.
Kangaroos can change direction suddenly, and where there is one there are often more.
Road trains, trucks towing several trailers, can stretch beyond 50 metres.
Pass only with a long, clear view ahead.
If one approaches on a narrow road, slow down and move left.
On gravel, drive slower, avoid harsh braking and steering, and keep your headlights on in dust.
Check road conditions first, as roads may close after rain.
Remote breakdowns and help.
Before heading remote, tell someone your route and arrival time.
Carry far more water than you think you need, plus food, a first aid kit, a spare tyre and tools.
Mobile coverage vanishes across much of Australia, so many travellers carry a satellite device or personal locator beacon.
If you break down, stay with your vehicle.
It is far easier for searchers to spot than a person, and it gives shade.
People have died walking away in extreme heat.
After a crash, get clear of traffic and turn on your hazard lights.
Call Triple Zero, 000, if someone is hurt or trapped, a vehicle is on fire or the road is blocked.
The free Emergency+ app shows your GPS location to read to the operator.
A first aid course will prepare you to help.
The key idea: Country roads carry a disproportionate share of Australia's road deaths, and fatigue and distraction are the quiet killers on long drives.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What made the faulty heater in this case so dangerous?
Answer. The gas gives no smoke, smell or taste to warn you.
Question two. Why should anyone with a significant electric shock see a doctor even if they feel fine?
Answer. Skin wounds can hide serious internal damage.
Question three. Why are long country drives especially risky?
Answer. Higher speeds, fatigue and help being far away.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
